entry.content:
If you've ever dealt with big web apps, you know how painful it is to maintain massive, nested UI code. Web Components are here to save the day! They're a set of standards that let you create custom, reusable, self-contained components that work in any modern browser, whether you're rocking vanilla JavaScript or a trendy new framework.

While Angular, React, and Vue are awesome, understanding the basics of Web Components is crucial. Learning these standards first gives you the foundation you need to troubleshoot those framework abstractions later on. 

A key benefit is avoiding ecosystem lock-in! Web Components let code written in different frameworks talk to each other. That makes cross-team work and tech migrations way easier.

This is the first post in my Web Components series. For this initial article, I really want to dive into one crucial feature: how to properly isolate your component from the rest of the website.

Light DOM: A non encapsulated approach

When a component renders its content directly into the host element (instead of attaching a Shadow DOM tree), it uses the main DOM tree (Light DOM), resulting in zero style or structural encapsulation. The component catches all the global website styles, and its content is wide open to external JavaScript. 

<example-component></example-component>

<style>
  /* The component will inherit global styles */
  * {
    box-sizing: border-box;
  }
  body {
    margin: 1rem;
    font-family: system-ui, sans-serif;
  }
  /* We can apply styles to an element inside the Web Component */
  p {
    font-style: italic;
  }
  /* We can apply styles to the Web Component itself */
  component {
    display: block;
    border: 1px solid black;
    padding: 0 1rem;
  }
</style>

<script>
  // Declare Web Component class
  class LightDom extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
      super();
      this.#render();
      console.log('render');
    }
    #render() {
      this.innerHTML = `<p>Styles exposed.</p>`;
      console.log('innerHTML', this.innerHTML);
    }
  }
  // Register the HTML tag
  customElements.define('example-component', LightDom);
  // The component content can be modified with JavaScript
  document
    .getElementsByTagName('example-component')[0]
    .innerHTML += '<p>Accessible by JavaScript.</p>';
</script>

Relying on Light DOM limits your control over the component's look way too much. As your app scales, managing CSS specificity and avoiding style clashes becomes a huge headache. Plus, you'll be tempted to access the component's guts from outside. Watch out! That habit makes the internal structure super fragile and easy to break. ☠️

Open Shadow DOM: Partial style isolation, JS exposure

To get the isolation we need, we must use the Shadow DOM. It comes in two modes: open and closed. Let's check out the open mode first! 

<script>
  // Declare Web Component class
  class ShadowOpen extends HTMLElement {
    #dom = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' });
    constructor() {
      super();
      this.#render();
    }
    #render() {
      this.#dom.innerHTML = `<p>Styles partially isolated.</p>`;
    }
  } 
  // Register the HTML tag
  customElements.define('example-component', ShadowOpen);
  // The component content can be modified with JavaScript
  document
    .getElementsByTagName('example-component')[0]
    .shadowRoot
    .innerHTML += '<p>Accessible by JavaScript.</p>';
</script>

The host element exposes the “shadowRoot” property, so external code can still access and mess with its internal structure using JavaScript. 

Yep, the component still inherits some general styles (like the font family), and you can still style the main tag (like its border or padding). But you can't change the styles of elements inside the component anymore!

Closed Shadow DOM: JS isolation

The Closed Shadow DOM mode makes the component's internals completely inaccessible to outside JavaScript manipulation. 

<script>
  // Declare Web Component class
  class ShadowClosed extends HTMLElement {
    #dom = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'closed' });
    constructor() {
      super();
      this.#render();
    }
    #render() {
      this.#dom.innerHTML = `<p>Styles partially isolated.</p>`;
    }
  }
  // Register the HTML tag
  customElements.define('example-component', ShadowClosed);
  // We can not modify the component content with JavaScript
  const el = document.getElementsByTagName('example-component')[0];
  try {
    el.shadowRoot.innerHTML += '<p>Accessible by JavaScript.</p>';
  } catch (e) {
    el.insertAdjacentHTML(
      'afterend',
      '<p>Not accessible by JavaScript</p>'
    );
  }
</script>

Awesome! Our component is now structurally and programmatically protected. But a big challenge remains: style inheritance. What if you can't control the global styles of the website hosting your component? Maybe you're working with legacy code or building a widget to embed anywhere. You absolutely need to isolate your component's styles!

Achieving full encapsulation via style reset

The way to avoid unwanted inheritance is to apply a CSS Reset right inside the Shadow DOM thanks to the special ":host" selector. Think of it like putting the component in a protective bubble, ensuring your widget looks exactly as you designed it, no matter where it lands.  

<script>
  // Declare Web Component class
  class ResetStyles extends HTMLElement {
    #dom = this.attachShadow({ mode: 'closed' });
    constructor() {
      super();
      this.#render();
    }
    #render() {
      this.#dom.innerHTML = `
        <style>:host { all: initial !important; }</style>
        <p>Styles are now isolated.</p>
      `;
    }
  }
  // Register the HTML tag
  customElements.define('example-component', ResetStyles);
  // We can not modify the component content with JavaScript
  const el = document.getElementsByTagName('example-component')[0];
  // ...
</script>

With this approach, the website's stylesheet won't pollute your component's styles anymore. This guarantees your widget looks reliable and perfect! 🥳

Summary

Web Components provide a super powerful, standards-based foundation for making truly reusable UI elements. A key point when using them the encapsulation: Light DOM offers zero protection, but Shadow DOM is the native way to isolate things. By picking Open or Closed, you control JS access, and by using an aggressive CSS Reset, you ensure your styles are completely safe from external contamination!
